title: Former Iran President Rouhani Pushes Regional Support for US-Iran Peace Deal
excerpt: Hassan Rouhani urges neighboring countries to back the Tehran-Washington MOU as nuclear talks stall over Strait of Hormuz control and frozen assets.
body:
• Former Iranian President Hassan Rouhani is lobbying neighboring countries to guarantee and support the US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed on June 15, 2026.
  • The MOU commits both sides to ceasing military operations, initiating final deal negotiations within 60 days, and lifting the US naval blockade within 30 days.
  • Nuclear talks remain stalled as Iran's Foreign Minister Araqchi says Tehran will not negotiate while Washington breaches the interim deal.
  • The Revolutionary Guard's push to control the Strait of Hormuz and impose shipping fees is undermining President Pezeshkian's diplomatic efforts.

Former Iranian President Hassan Rouhani has launched a public campaign urging Iran's neighboring countries to endorse and help guarantee the memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington, arguing that the region's stability depends on the agreement's success.

The MOU, digitally signed on June 15, 2026, represents the most significant diplomatic channel between Iran and the United States in years. A formal signing ceremony is expected in Geneva, though no date has been confirmed. Rouhani's intervention comes as implementation has stalled and tensions between the two sides have escalated over the Strait of Hormuz.

Three Pillars of the MOU

The agreement rests on three core commitments. First, both sides pledged to cease military operations, with specific attention to Lebanon. Second, the governments agreed to initiate negotiations on a final comprehensive deal within 60 days of signing. Third, the US naval blockade is to be lifted within 30 days.

The 30-day blockade deadline represented the most immediate and verifiable concession from Washington. However, disputes over implementation—particularly around the Strait of Hormuz—have thrown the timeline into doubt.

Rouhani's Diplomatic Playbook

Rouhani's regional lobbying is consistent with the diplomatic philosophy he championed during his presidency from 2013 to 2021. He oversaw the negotiation of the 2015 nuclear deal (JCPOA) and built his political identity around constructive engagement with the international community.

"If neighboring countries actively endorse and participate in guaranteeing the MOU, it becomes harder for either side to walk away without broader diplomatic consequences."

— Analysis of Rouhani's regional lobbying strategy

His argument to regional capitals is straightforward: if neighboring countries actively back the MOU, it becomes far more difficult for either Washington or Tehran to abandon the agreement without facing broader diplomatic fallout. Without regional buy-in, the deal remains a fragile bilateral arrangement at the mercy of domestic politics in both capitals.

Stalled Negotiations

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on August 9 that Tehran and Washington are not currently engaged in talks, and that Iran will not resume negotiations as long as Washington breaches the interim deal. He confirmed that messages continue to be exchanged through intermediaries.

Araqchi repeated Iran's position that an agreement on the Strait of Hormuz between Tehran and Muscat is in its "final stages" but would not reopen the strategic waterway immediately. The agreement would set out new shipping lanes to be used once the US fulfills other conditions.

Power Struggle in Tehran

The domestic reaction in Iran has been sharply divided. President Masoud Pezeshkian, elected on a pledge to revive Iran's economy and encourage engagement with the West, has framed the MOU as "a great victory for the Iranian people" and pointed to $6 billion in frozen assets held in Qatar that could be released under the agreement.

But the Revolutionary Guard, which controls the naval force patrolling Iranian waters, views the Strait of Hormuz as a valuable strategic asset. Guard officials have pushed to establish a mechanism to impose fees for passage through the strait, which Iranian officials say could generate $40 billion annually. This directly conflicts with the MOU's provision for free passage.

The tension between Pezeshkian's diplomatic priorities and the Guard's strategic calculations has been described by analysts as the central obstacle to implementing the peace deal.

What's Next

The 60-day negotiation window from the MOU's June signing has effectively elapsed without formal nuclear talks beginning. Sensitive issues including uranium enrichment, highly enriched materials, and comprehensive sanctions removal have all been deferred to a second phase that has yet to start. Whether Rouhani's regional lobbying can generate enough multilateral pressure to restart the process remains the key question for the region's diplomatic future.
